chapter_title: Fit Body, Fit Mind, Fit Nation
subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 9 periods = 360 minutes
Total: 9 periods · 6h 0min

periods.section_title: Fit Body, Fit Mind, Fit Nation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Read (pp.67–68): teacher-led read-aloud of the full poem with new-word attention.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes the title 'Fit Body, Fit Mind, Fit Nation' on the board and invites students to say one sport or activity they enjoy, briefly collecting three or four responses to warm up listening.

Let us Read (pp.67–68): teacher reads the poem aloud in a clear, energetic voice, pausing at each child's name and quality descriptor — Active Anant, Graceful Geeta, Little Lhamo, Swift Shabana, musical Meena — so students hear the alliterative pattern before meeting the new words.

Teacher writes the six new words — mistakes, proudly, pace, rhythm, cheerful, swift — on the board one at a time, pronounces each clearly, uses it in a sentence drawn from the poem, and invites students to repeat the word together.
Choral reading: teacher and students read the poem aloud together twice, with the class echoing each triplet or couplet after the teacher, building fluency and confidence in pronunciation.

periods.teacher_notes: The alliterative quality descriptors are the poem's most distinctive feature — stress the matching initial sounds gently so students notice the pattern without being told its name yet. The word 'rhythm' often causes pronunciation difficulty; model it slowly (ri-thm) and have students tap a desk beat as they say it.

periods.section_title: Fit Body, Fit Mind, Fit Nation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think B (p.69): discuss all four comprehension questions about the poem's characters and details.

time_bands.activity: Quick paired chant: students read the poem aloud in pairs from Textbook pp. 67–68, one partner reading one stanza each, to reactivate the text before discussion begins.

Let us Think B (p.69): teacher reads Question 1 aloud ('Which game does Anant play?') and Question 2 ('Which musical instruments are mentioned?'), and students locate answers in the text, calling out responses and pointing to the stanza that supports each answer.

Let us Think B (p.69): teacher poses Questions 3 and 4 ('Who likes moving in rhythm?' and 'Who learns from skating mistakes?'), guiding students to read the relevant stanzas aloud before giving their answers in a full sentence.
Class reviews all four answers together; teacher writes a one-phrase summary of each answer on the board so students can self-check and correct their own responses before the unit closes.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes confuse Meena (singing in rhythm) with Lhamo (playing music); asking them to point to the exact stanza before answering prevents guessing. Encourage full-sentence answers ('Anant plays hockey') rather than single-word responses to build oral sentence construction.

periods.section_title: Fit Body, Fit Mind, Fit Nation
periods.activity_title: Think and Discuss — Sports, Music and Dance

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think C (p.69): guided discussion on school games, indoor/outdoor preference, musical instruments, and regional dance.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly recaps the five children from the poem — naming each with their activity — and tells the class they will now talk about their own favourite games and arts, connecting the poem's world to their own.

Let us Think C (p.69): teacher poses Questions 1 and 2 ('Which game do you play in school?' and 'Indoor or outdoor game — which do you enjoy more?'); students discuss in pairs for one minute, then three or four pairs share with the class, with the teacher extending each response with a follow-up such as 'Why do you like it?'

Let us Think C (p.69): teacher poses Questions 3 and 4 about musical instruments; students share instruments they have seen or played, and the teacher lists named instruments on the board, celebrating the variety the class produces.

Let us Think C (p.69): teacher poses Question 5 on dance forms; students name their favourite dance and a famous regional dance, and the teacher acknowledges the cultural diversity that emerges, closing by reminding the class that the poem celebrates exactly this variety.

periods.teacher_notes: Students may be shy to speak about personal preferences; phrasing questions as 'Who in your family plays an instrument?' can lower the barrier before asking about themselves. Accept answers in students' home language where needed and help them find the English word together.

periods.section_title: Fit Body, Fit Mind, Fit Nation
periods.activity_title: Alliteration and Adjectives — Discovering Describing Words

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think A (p.69): write one quality beginning with the same letter as your own name, using the poem's alliterative pattern.
Let us Learn A (p.70): match adjectives (blue, hardworking, green, pebbled, healthy) to their nouns.

time_bands.activity: Let us Think A (p.69): teacher writes 'Active Anant' and 'Graceful Geeta' on the board, underlines the first letters, and asks students to notice the pattern; students then write one quality that starts with the same letter as their own name and share with a partner.

Teacher draws out the idea that these quality words tell us more about the person; she introduces the word 'adjective' by writing it on the board with the definition and three examples from the poem, helping students connect the term to what they just practised.

Let us Learn A (p.70): teacher reads each adjective aloud ('blue', 'hardworking', 'green', 'pebbled', 'healthy'), invites students to suggest a noun it could describe before revealing the textbook pairs, then students complete the matching task in their books.

Pairs check each other's matching answers; teacher reviews each pair on the board ('blue — sky', 'hardworking — children') and asks students to say a new sentence using each adjective+noun pair aloud, reinforcing the concept through oral production.

periods.teacher_notes: The alliteration task (Task A) is a warm, personal entry into adjectives; avoid over-correcting students' chosen quality words — the goal is generating a meaningful describing word, not finding the 'right' answer. For the matching task, students who confuse 'pebbled road' and 'green leaves' benefit from hearing the combinations aloud rather than correcting silently.

periods.section_title: Fit Body, Fit Mind, Fit Nation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn B (p.70): fill blanks with nouns for given adjectives and vice versa.
Let us Write D (p.72): find rhyming words from the poem for hockey, skates, guitar, race, joy.

time_bands.activity: Let us Learn B (p.70): teacher writes 'happy ___' on the board and elicits several possible nouns from the class, then students individually complete all four adjective+noun blanks and all four ___+noun blanks in their books before sharing answers aloud.

Teacher reviews Let us Learn B answers by calling on individual students; for each answer, she asks 'Is that a describing word or a naming word?' to keep the adjective/noun distinction active before moving to the rhyming task.

Let us Write D (p.72): teacher reads each target word aloud (hockey, skates, guitar, race, joy) with an extended final sound so students hear the rhyme signal, then students open Textbook pp. 67–68 and scan the poem to find and write the rhyming partner for each word.
Quick class check: teacher calls out each target word and students chorus the rhyming answer ('hockey — rocky!', 'skates — mistakes!') to confirm all five rhyme pairs before the unit closes.

periods.teacher_notes: For Let us Learn B, accept any grammatically plausible noun ('happy child', 'happy day') — the task builds productive flexibility, not a single correct answer. When hunting rhymes in the poem, some students scan visually rather than listening for the sound; encourage them to read the stanza quietly to themselves to hear the rhyme before writing.

periods.section_title: Fit Body, Fit Mind, Fit Nation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write C (p.72): match five words (Brave, Rocky, Mistakes, Proudly, Delightful) to their meanings.

homework.task_brief: Let us Write D (p.72): write the five rhyming pairs in a sentence each, using the poem's context as a guide.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes the five words — Brave, Rocky, Mistakes, Proudly, Delightful — on the board and asks students to predict, in their own words, what each might mean, accepting any reasonable guess and noting it without correction yet.

Let us Write C (p.72): teacher reads each definition aloud from the textbook ('Feeling happy about something you did well', 'Courageous and bold', etc.) and students discuss in pairs which word fits before writing their answers in the circles.

Class reviews answers; for each matched word the teacher returns to the poem line where it appears ('proudly plays a guitar', 'even when the ground is rocky') and reads it aloud, so students see the word in its original context and confirm or correct their match.

Students choose two of the five words and say an original sentence aloud using each word, with the teacher offering brief feedback on meaning and usage, consolidating the vocabulary in active oral production.

periods.teacher_notes: The word 'Proudly' can be confused with 'happily' at this stage because both carry positive feeling; returning to Lhamo's stanza — where he plays guitar proudly — helps students feel the difference between manner and mood. The homework asks students to write rhyming pairs in sentences; keep the instruction short and point them to the poem page so they have the words in front of them.

periods.section_title: Fit Body, Fit Mind, Fit Nation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write A (p.71): fill three blanks with double-letter words using the parrot picture as prompt.
Let us Write B (p.71): brainstorm and write five kitchen items with double letters.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes 'village' on the board, underlines the 'll', and explains that 'double letters' are two of the same letter sitting side by side; she invites students to say any word they know with double letters and lists five or six on the board to warm up the concept.

Let us Write A (p.71): teacher directs students to the parrot picture on p.71, reads the sentence frame aloud ('This is my pet ___. It loves to eat ___, which are ___ in colour'), and the class discusses possible double-letter words (parrot, carrot, green) before students write their answers in the blanks.

Let us Write B (p.71): teacher leads a quick brainstorm by asking 'What do you see in your kitchen at home?' and students call out items; together the class checks which ones have double letters (butter, coffee, pepper, egg, bottle, spoon), with the teacher guiding the checking strategy — say the word, write it, look for twins.

Students write their five kitchen items in their books; pairs exchange books to verify that each word genuinely contains a double letter, then the teacher takes two or three volunteers to share their lists aloud, celebrating variety and correcting gently where needed.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often choose 'egg' but are unsure whether two different letters at the end (g+g) count — affirm that they do, as the concept is two identical letters together. The kitchen brainstorm can yield culturally varied words; accept local food words alongside English ones and help students find the English spelling.

periods.section_title: Fit Body, Fit Mind, Fit Nation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Do (p.71): organise a 'Preparing a Dish Without Fire' activity and share the dish with the class.

time_bands.activity: Teacher connects to the poem's theme by asking: 'The poem talks about fit, cheerful children — what kind of food helps us stay fit and cheerful?' and takes four or five responses to link healthy eating to the poem's message before introducing the activity.

Let us Do (p.71): teacher explains the 'Preparing a Dish Without Fire' task — students will prepare a simple no-cook dish (fruit chaat, cucumber slices with lemon, banana milkshake) in groups of four using ingredients and tools available in class or brought from home today.

Groups prepare their dishes; teacher circulates, assisting with cutting, mixing, and portioning, ensuring safety with any sharp tools, and encouraging students to name each ingredient and describe what they are doing using simple sentences.

Each group presents their dish to the class in two or three sentences: what it is, what is in it, and why it is healthy; the class tastes and the teacher closes by returning to the poem — 'Just like Anant, Geeta, and the others, preparing healthy food is also part of a fit and joyful life.'

periods.teacher_notes: Coordinate with school administration in advance if ingredients need to come from home; a fallback is a fruit-only or biscuit-and-fruit combination that avoids allergen concerns. The presentation step (each group naming their dish) is the language goal — ensure every group speaks, not just shows.

periods.section_title: Fit Body, Fit Mind, Fit Nation
periods.activity_title: Paralympic Games — Research, Share and Celebrate

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Explore (p.72): find out about the Paralympic Games and share key points with the class.

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks: 'The poem says playing is a joy for every girl and boy — do you think children and people with disabilities can play sport too?' Takes responses and introduces the word 'Paralympic' by writing it on the board.

Let us Explore (p.72): teacher shares four or five key facts about the Paralympic Games — what they are, when they started, which sports are included, and one or two notable Indian Paralympians — using pictures or a poster if available, building a shared knowledge base the class will draw on in their sharing.

Students work in pairs to discuss and prepare two sentences each: one fact about the Paralympic Games and one sentence about why they find it inspiring; teacher circulates, prompting pairs who are quiet with questions like 'What surprised you most about what I shared?'

Pairs share with the class in a brief oral presentation; teacher records the class's key points in a list on the board, then closes the unit by returning to the poem's final lines — 'Cheerful children everywhere, playing is a joy! for every girl and boy' — reading them aloud as a collective celebration.

periods.teacher_notes: Students may not have heard of the Paralympic Games before; the teacher-led fact-sharing in the middle band is essential scaffolding, not optional. Connecting a named Indian Paralympian (such as Devendra Jhajharia or Avani Lekhara) to the poem's spirit of joyful participation makes the exploration feel real and motivating.
materials: Pictures or poster of Paralympic Games (optional)
Reference book or printed facts on Paralympic Games

items.item_stem: Read the lines on page 67 beginning "Swift girl Shabana". What did Shabana win, and how did she feel afterwards?

options.label: A
options.text: She won a cycle race and happily celebrated her fastest pace.

options.label: B
options.text: She won a guitar contest and played proudly.

options.label: C
options.text: She won a hockey match and felt proud.

options.label: D
options.text: She won a skating competition and learned from her mistakes.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Student may be mixing up Shabana's stanza with Anant's hockey verse.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student has confused Shabana with Geeta, who skates and learns from mistakes.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student has confused Shabana with Lhamo, who plays guitar proudly.

items.item_stem: Two of the five children in the poem make music rather than play sport. Who are they, and what instruments does the poem say they play? Write your answer in one or two sentences.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Lhamo plays the guitar, and his friend plays the sitar. These are the two musical children in the poem.

items.source_context: Favourite school games, indoor vs outdoor play, musical instruments seen or played, regional dance forms.
items.item_stem: The poem celebrates both sport and music. Listen to these two statements and decide whether each one is true or false: (1) Playing an outdoor game and playing an indoor game are both ways of enjoying yourself. (2) You can only like sport OR music — not both at the same time.

options.text: Playing an outdoor game and playing an indoor game are both ways of enjoying yourself.
You can only like sport OR music — not both at the same time.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Statement 1 is true — the poem celebrates all kinds of play, indoor and outdoor. Statement 2 is false — the poem itself shows Lhamo playing guitar alongside Shabana racing, and Meena singing, so the children enjoy both sport and music.
